title: Portfolio prioritization & starts control
subtitle: How to govern what enters the active pipeline so the work that starts actually finishes
core_thesis: Most product organizations start more projects than they can finish. The cure is not better execution. It is a portfolio discipline that ranks every candidate against weighted strategic and economic criteria, then gates entry to the active pipeline against real resource capacity. Rank without constraints first. Apply constraints second. One person owns the call. Starting fewer projects is how more projects finish on time.
abstract: Most product organizations start more projects than they can finish. This paper describes the lateralworks FTTM portfolio discipline: AHP-based ranking that orders candidates by strategic and economic value without constraints, then a six-step zero-based budgeting loop that applies real resource capacity to determine what actually starts. The discipline draws on independent research from Saaty, Cooper, Reinertsen, Goldratt, Wheelwright and Clark, and Rogers and Blenko — converging on the same conclusion: rank rigorously, gate against capacity, name a single Decider.

title: The optimal project load
subtitle: How dedicated resources accelerate new product development
core_thesis: One to two projects per engineer is the maximum sustainable load for complex new product development; past two, context switching consumes 40 to 75 percent of working time, queue delays compound at every milestone gate, and calendars slip by months — the structural fix is dedicated cross-functional product teams governed by an explicit portfolio and clear decision rights.
abstract: Most semiconductor organizations spread their best engineers across three to five projects on the theory that high utilization equals high productivity. Four decades of research from Weinberg, Reinertsen, Brooks, Clark and Wheelwright, and McKinsey says the opposite. Past two concurrent projects, context switching consumes 40 to 75 percent of working time and queue delays compound nonlinearly. The structural answer is dedicated cross-functional product teams limited to one or two projects per engineer, governed by an explicit portfolio and clear decision rights.

title: Managing the fuzzy front end
subtitle: Where the biggest schedule opportunity hides — and how to capture it through dedicated teams, a refreshed schedule, and a hard cycle-time target
core_thesis: The fuzzy front end is the largest, cheapest, and least-managed source of schedule slip in technology product development. Treat it as a real project — with a dedicated cross-functional team, a weekly-refreshed schedule, and a hard cycle-time target — and months come out of the development calendar without compressing the engineering work that follows.
abstract: Most product development organizations spend 50 to 100 percent of their cycle time in a phase they do not manage. The fuzzy front end — between portfolio commit and full-team formation — is owned by no one in particular and runs without a schedule. This paper diagnoses the structural causes of FFE drift, generalizes Sun Microsystems' six-week cycle-time discipline into a seven-practice methodology, maps the two handoffs that bookend it, and walks the implementation sequence. A current semiconductor engagement illustrates the failure mode and the recovery.

title: fastProjectAI Project Portfolio Dashboard
subtitle: Aggregating live project schedules into a single leadership view
core_thesis: Most leadership teams running multiple programs cannot see their portfolio in time to act. fastProjectAI fixes this by aggregating live wigglechart data the PMs already maintain — surfacing the small number of projects that need attention this week, not the long tail that does not.
abstract: How leadership teams running multiple new-product programs can replace status-report theater with live, exception-based portfolio visibility — drawn from data their PMs already maintain as part of FTTM planning. Walks through the architecture, the filtering model, the free-data argument, a worked example from a site-deployment program, and an LLM-driven cross-portfolio pattern detection layer.

title: FTTM Process Maturity
subtitle: A framework for measuring and improving team performance
core_thesis: A team’s schedule maturity is observable, measurable, and migratable. Teams move through four levels — from ML0 (no schedule) to ML3 (active acceleration) — by changing specific behaviors in the weekly refresh. Knowing where a team sits on this curve is the prerequisite to changing it.
abstract: A measurement framework for the FTTM methodology, with definitions of the four maturity levels, a 30-criterion self-assessment scorecard, migration guidance, and the seven factors that determine how quickly teams advance. Near-relative of the Capability Maturity Model from Carnegie Mellon’s Software Engineering Institute, focused specifically on the weekly schedule refresh and explicitly connecting maturity to acceleration.

title: Host best practices
subtitle: How executives create the conditions for fast product development
core_thesis: Teams deliver products; the host creates the conditions under which they deliver fast. Fix the host and speed becomes the default. Leave the host alone and team-level improvement fades within a year.
abstract: The 13 host practices that lateralworks has found, across more than three decades of consulting with technology companies, separate fast organizations from slow ones. The practices fall into three groups: the mindset executives hold about speed, the environment they build around teams, and the portfolio of projects they manage. Each practice is presented as a contrast: what normal organizations do, and what fast ones do differently. Includes an anonymized storage-technology case study and an empowerment matrix.

title: Team best practices
subtitle: How fast teams get the right product to market at the right time
core_thesis: A fast team organizes itself around the customer (right-product), assembles the smallest competent group of role-owners (right-team), and uses its schedule as the primary tool for driving decisions and exposing gaps (right-time). Inside a provisioning host, these 15 practices cut time-to-market by 30 to 50 percent.
abstract: The 15 team practices that operate inside a healthy host. Right-product covers six practices for getting the team to a product customers actually want and will pay for. Right-team covers two practices for turning a roster of names into a team that can deliver. Right-time covers seven practices for turning a schedule from a reporting artifact into a tool the team uses every day. Companion to Host best practices.

title: Managing up, managing down, and the innovation paradox
subtitle: Why senior-manager failure modes kill the innovation their organizations depend on
core_thesis: Innovation needs encouragement before scrutiny, but most organizations evaluate too early and kill fragile ideas. Senior managers either over-invest in managing up (optimizing the upward narrative) or over-invest in managing down (deep in operational weeds). Both break the protection-from-above the innovation environment depends on.
abstract: A synthesis of the innovation-environment framework and the senior-manager failure-mode framework, with a representative case study. Examines the two ways senior managers fail the innovation environment their companies depend on, the consequences that unfold on different timelines, and the structural patterns shared by companies that solve the paradox across decades — Google, 3M, Amazon, Pixar, Toyota, Analog Devices.

title: FTTM Product Development Best Practices
subtitle: Three decades of fast-team research, 2018 revision
core_thesis: FTTM outcomes are a function of two inputs — the behavior of the team and the environment within which the team operates. Best practices observed across hundreds of programs are codified into a Mindset / Host / Team framework that delivers the right product at the right time.
abstract: lateralworks Fast-Time-to-Market (FTTM) Practices, first researched in Silicon Valley in the early 1990s, are based on an ongoing worldwide study into the drivers of new product development success. This 2018 revision codifies practices observed across hundreds of teams into a three-axis framework — Mindset, Host, Team — applied across Portfolio, Environment, and Execution. It contrasts 'normal' team behavior with the practices that separate fast from slow.

title: Voice of the customer
subtitle: How fast teams figure out what to build and when it has to ship, and why the answer keeps moving while they build it.
core_thesis: Right-product is determined first, not last. Voice of the customer is how fast teams figure out what 'right' means today, then again next month, and again until the program ships. Programs that freeze the requirements early ship the wrong product into the right window, or the right product into the wrong one.
abstract: Most product programs that miss their market window do not miss because the engineering is slow — they miss because the team built the wrong thing, or built the right thing for a customer who has moved on. This paper sets out lateralworks' four-step Wants/Translation/Solution/Refresh loop, the AHP machinery for ranking customer wants and product hows defensibly, and the refresh cadence that keeps both current. Two anonymized case studies show the methodology applied end to end.

title: The management gap
subtitle: Twenty years of compounding technology innovation outran the way technology programs are managed. The lateralworks case studies show what works instead.
core_thesis: Technology capability has grown by orders of magnitude since 2005. The way technology programs are managed has not. Agile sped up feedback loops inside software teams but did not fix the structural problems that make complex programs late. The lateralworks FTTM methodology, refined since 1988 across 200+ programs, is the documented exception. The case studies are the evidence.
abstract: Programs that miss their market window usually do not miss because the engineering is slow. They miss because the operating model that organizes the work was built for a slower era. Between 2005 and 2025 the underlying technology stack moved by orders of magnitude — compute per dollar, transistor density, network throughput, and now generative AI compute. Mainstream program management did not. The paper walks the gap, the Agile evidence, the FTTM research base, and two field-tested case studies.

title: Learning cycles
subtitle: How to predict and accelerate advanced technology development
core_thesis: Innovation is not random. The duration of a breakthrough can be approximated by counting learning cycles and multiplying by typical cycle time, sized against problem difficulty. Programs accelerate by working two levers in parallel: more cycles running concurrently and shorter cycle time per cycle.
abstract: A practical method for predicting and accelerating breakthroughs in advanced technology development. Built on T.J. Rodgers's easy/hard/difficult sizing model and refined across 200+ lateralworks engagements since 1988. Classify each problem, estimate cycles and cycle time, then close the schedule gap with two levers: concurrency and cycle-time compression. Includes fast-team behaviors, weekly refresh planning, isolation of breakthrough work, and learning milestones. Programs that adopt the full method routinely deliver advanced technology in 60–70 percent of original schedule estimates.

title: 10 best practices of fast teams
subtitle: Ten proven practices that consistently move products to market faster
core_thesis: Fast time to market is not the result of working harder. It comes from ten disciplined practices, installed together, that turn the schedule into a living instrument and the team into its owner. Speed is not an outcome — it is a habit, protected one Tuesday morning at a time.
abstract: Speed is a cultural asset, not a tooling choice. Over thirty-six years of multi-company research and 200+ client engagements, lateralworks has identified a consistent set of practices that distinguish teams who deliver the right product at the right time from teams who do not. This paper presents ten practices — drawn from the thirty-one documented in FTTM New Product Development Best Practices, Revision 2018.002 — chosen because they compound. A team that installs all ten owns the minimum viable FTTM operating system.

title: Bring pain forward
subtitle: Happy schedules, the gap, and the discipline of finding reality early
core_thesis: Three practices share a single discipline: bring reality forward in time so the team can act on it. Accelerate the pain so urgency arrives early. Build a schedule honest enough to expose the gap. Track the trend so you see slippage before it lands. Each practice fails on its own without a host environment that rewards early honesty.
abstract: Most development projects do not fail because the team lacked skill. They fail because the team did not see the failure coming until it was too late to act. The gap between target and reality already existed. Nobody named it. By the time the milestone review surfaced the slip, the cheap options were gone. This paper describes three connected practices good product organizations use to keep that from happening — bring pain forward, drop the happy schedule, and know the gap — and the host conditions that let them stick. Used together, they form the discipline lateralworks calls before-the-fact behavior.

title: Common problems in advanced technology programs
subtitle: Four failure patterns we keep seeing — and why traditional project management cannot solve them.
core_thesis: Advanced technology programs do not fail because the work is too hard. They fail because four organizational patterns — distributed sites, multiple companies, multiple corporate stakeholders, and simultaneous innovation with product development — overwhelm conventional project management. FTTM is the operating system built for these conditions.
abstract: Most advanced technology programs miss their dates for the same handful of reasons. After 36 years and 200+ lateralworks engagements, four problem patterns recur: multi-site distribution, multi-company partnerships, multiple corporate stakeholders, and simultaneous innovation with product development. The paper names each pattern, gives a diagnostic table for recognizing it inside a program, and pairs it with the FTTM practices that resolve it. The second half makes a sharper claim — FTTM is not a flavor of project management. The two operate from opposite premises: project management controls variance against a plan; FTTM compresses the time between learning and decision.

title: Critical thinking and the challenge process
subtitle: How fast teams question assumptions to close schedule gaps and break through technical problems
core_thesis: A late schedule is not only a tracking problem. It is a thinking problem. When a team treats its current plan as fixed, the only moves left are to admit defeat or to cut the product. Challenge opens a third move: question the assumptions behind the plan, then find a faster way to reach the same goal. Used deliberately, it turns a schedule gap into the pressure that produces a breakthrough.
abstract: Most teams meet a slipping schedule by working harder inside the plan or cutting scope to fit the date. Both leave the underlying assumptions untouched. This paper sets out the challenge process: a structured way to surface the assumptions behind a plan, ask why each is held, and convert the weak ones into faster paths that still meet the goal. The same loop that closes a schedule gap breaks the technical problems hiding behind it.

title: Four questions every product leader should ask
subtitle: Heavyweight teams, real empowerment, pulling pain forward, and the trouble with happy schedules
core_thesis: The four questions look like separate topics — team design, delegation, risk timing, and scheduling. They are one topic. Speed comes from a team that owns the outcome, an explicit envelope of authority that lets it act without asking, a culture that surfaces problems early, and a schedule the team believes and the organization can trust. Remove any one and the other three lose their force.
abstract: Four questions separate fast product organizations from slow ones: what a heavyweight team actually is, what empowerment means once you make it precise, why high performers pull their pain forward instead of avoiding it, and whether you want a happy schedule or a realistic one. Each has an easy answer that sounds reasonable and is wrong. This paper takes the harder answer in every case, grounded in FTTM practice and the research behind it.

title: Before the fact leadership
subtitle: Building organizations that anticipate problems — and hiring the C-suite that will
core_thesis: The happy schedule is the blue pill; the reality-based schedule is the red pill. Anticipation is not a personality trait — it is a behavior the organization either rewards or punishes, and that C-suite leaders either model or suppress.
abstract: Most organizations reward the wrong behavior. The leader who surfaces a problem six months early gets labeled negative; the leader who saves the launch at the last minute gets promoted. This paper names the pattern, shows why it is structurally stable, and describes the three layers — culture, process, and Freedom Level 1 delegation — by which CEOs reverse it. Closes with a structured interview framework for hiring C-suite leaders who already practice before-the-fact behavior.

title: Systems thinkers: where did they go?
subtitle: How complexity outran integration — and why technology programs still slip, overrun, and break at the seams
core_thesis: Modern program failure is not a shortage of engineering talent or project-management software. It is the absence of two roles — the systems architect and the systems planner — that once owned the integrated whole; complexity grew while the integrators disappeared, and the slips and integration failures we treat as unavoidable are the predictable result.
abstract: Systems engineering was invented in the 1960s to manage machines too complex for any one person to hold in their head — and a pair of dedicated roles, the systems architect and the systems planner, owned the integrated whole. Those roles have quietly disappeared while complexity exploded. This paper traces the decline, quantifies what integration failure costs, and prescribes the cure: restore the two roles, give them authority, and pair them at program kickoff.

title: Cut smart, not everywhere
subtitle: Priority-based budget optimization for resource-constrained programs — how AHP decision models protect mission-critical spending and eliminate waste.
core_thesis: Every dollar is an investment in the company's primary objective: spending that accelerates the mission is protected, and spending that does not is cut. A structured decision model makes the distinction explicit, defensible, and immune to the politics that turn most cost programs into across-the-board reductions.
abstract: Equal cuts treat mission-critical investment and discretionary overhead as the same line, and most fail. This paper replaces across-the-board reductions with the Analytic Hierarchy Process: every spending category is rated against three weighted criteria — cost, mission value, and time-to-market impact — and ranked protect, invest, review, or cut. Intel's $10B indiscriminate cut and Apple's surgical optimization under Cook frame the contrast. The full exercise runs in a three-hour executive session and produces a ranking the CFO can defend to the board.

title: The scheduling debate
subtitle: Truth-based planning versus top-down targets
core_thesis: The debate between aggressive and realistic scheduling is a false dichotomy; the real question is who owns the plan. When the people doing the work own the schedule they fight to deliver it, and when leadership imposes it the gap between target and reality goes underground — surfacing late, expensively, and without warning.
abstract: Every development organization faces the same conflict: leadership wants aggressive timelines, and the experts doing the work know what delivery actually requires. The two camps are not arguing about the same artifact — one defends the target, the other the plan. Aggressive targets are healthy, but they must sit beside honest plans built by the people who execute them. Surfaced and managed, the gap between target and plan closes. Hidden, it surfaces on its own schedule, at a cost no one budgeted.

title: The innovation paradox
subtitle: How to build a culture where new ideas are both encouraged and stress-tested without being killed
core_thesis: Strong ideas arrive rough and need room to develop before judgment. The same rigor that makes a company good at execution can kill ideas in their fragile state — so the leader's job is to sequence the work: support first, scrutiny second, refinement throughout.
abstract: Six companies, one structural problem, and a model leaders can run on Monday. Grounded in Harvard Business School research on psychological safety and in lateralworks field practice across 200+ technology programs since 1988.

title: Right product, right time
subtitle: How an honest schedule reveals whether you are building the right thing, in time to do something about it
core_thesis: Every program carries three truths — the market's target, the schedule the team can deliver, and the requirements that define the product — and most organizations collapse them into a single date. The schedule is the only one that produces a measurable signal every week, so an honest schedule is the first truth to break the silence and force the harder question: are we building the right thing at all?
abstract: A lateralworks methodology paper on right-time product development. An anonymized AI-datacenter memory program shows how building an honest schedule surfaced a five-year reality hiding behind a two-year wish, and how that one truth forced the requirements and the roadmap back into alignment with the market. Connects the practice to the literature on cost of delay, the planning fallacy, strategic misrepresentation, and time-to-market economics.

title: The FTTM core team
subtitle: Roles, not functions: how heavyweight, lateralized teams become the single greatest contributor to development speed
core_thesis: A cross-functional core team is not a group of functions assigned to a project. The FTTM core team carries three critical roles at its center — a chief engineer, a product leader who is the voice of the customer, and a system architect — held together by a heavyweight technical program manager who acts as the integrator. Those roles pull the whole program sideways, across the functional walls, from first definition to final delivery. That lateral pull is what produces speed. Of everything a company can change to get to market faster, the team is the largest single lever.
abstract: Speed in product development is decided by how a program is organized, not how hard people work. This paper is a deep dive into one structure: the FTTM core team — a small, dedicated, role-based team led by a heavyweight integrator, empowered to own the outcome end to end. Placing it inside the Wheelwright–Clark team typology and Reinertsen's economics of flow, it shows why roles, not functions — the lateralization of programs — is the single greatest lever on time to market.

title: Starts control
subtitle: Balancing the portfolio for speed
core_thesis: The active project portfolio is a zero-sum game. Best-practice companies balance it deliberately: manage the fuzzy front end on a clock, rank every candidate against weighted business objectives, and gate each start against real resource capacity. When one project is added, another is killed or deprioritized. Organizations that skip this discipline overload the engineers already carrying the committed portfolio and deliver everything late.
abstract: Speed is decided at the portfolio, before any project team is formed. This paper examines how uncontrolled project starts produce too many projects, the wrong projects, and not enough resources — and how best-practice companies put a clock on the fuzzy front end, rank every candidate against weighted business objectives, and gate each start against real resource capacity. Full-length follow-on to the lateralworks briefing Portfolio prioritization & starts control, drawn from FTTM field research and four decades of portfolio literature.

title: The long pole
subtitle: Find the path that sets the end date, challenge the assumptions holding it up, and whittle it down every week
core_thesis: The long pole sets the end date. Most organizations watch it grow; fast teams cut it down. Find the real long pole, challenge the assumptions that hold up its duration, cut in big chunks without letting the tent fall down, and whittle it every week through refresh planning. Do this and the end date becomes something the team sets, not something it discovers.
abstract: Every project has one path that decides when it ends. This paper sets out the lateralworks long pole method: find the real long pole and the honest gap to target, determine what makes it that long, challenge the assumptions holding up its duration and cut in big chunks, then whittle weekly through refresh planning. Evidence runs through a semiconductor fab wigglechart — a predicted two-year slip pulled back to first silicon two weeks early — plus learning-cycle estimation for invention work.

title: Make your bed
subtitle: The non-negotiable weekly refresh, and why cadence is the one thing your team can always control
core_thesis: The weekly schedule refresh is your project's made bed — the one event whose existence depends only on the team's own discipline. Run on a fixed three-day rhythm, it produces a specific pull-in decision every week and turns the schedule from a record of the past into an instrument for changing the outcome.
abstract: Admiral McRaven told graduates to start every day by making their bed — not for tidiness, but for agency. This paper draws a direct line from that lesson to the weekly schedule refresh: the one event a development team controls absolutely. It codifies the three-day operating rhythm from honest task-owner updates through critical-path analysis to a forty-minute pull-in meeting, grounds the cadence in behavioral research on small wins and habit formation, and reproduces a complete AI-generated weekly status report from a live program.

title: Change control
subtitle: How empowered core teams govern the frozen specification and protect the launch date
core_thesis: Time to market and change control are the same subject. Every change to a frozen specification carries a schedule cost and a financial cost, and an organization that cannot price those costs will accept every change and miss every date. The fastest organizations give one small board authority over the specification, arm it with a live schedule and a cost-of-delay model, and make that board the core team itself.
abstract: Late products rarely die from one big decision — they bleed out through small, unpriced ones. This paper treats change control as a time-to-market discipline: a frozen specification under revision control, a change control board that is the only route by which the baseline moves, and a cost-of-delay model that converts schedule days into dollars. In the FTTM model the CCB is the core team itself, operating at freedom level 1 or 2 — it decides, then informs. Evidence from Boeing, Maersk Line, and Hewlett-Packard, closing with a practical two-page charter.

title: The Product Boss
subtitle: Roles and responsibilities in the Product Delivery Team model
core_thesis: The Product Boss exists to take a product from concept to market as fast as possible. They are the enforcement arm of the operational product strategy and the embodiment of FTTM at the product level. Without one person owning each product end to end, the program can define policies but cannot ensure compliance.
abstract: No one owns a product end to end. That is the finding behind this paper: functional swimlanes work as a planning framework and fail as an execution model, because no single person carries a product through NPI, qualification, and volume ramp. The Product Boss closes the gap as the CEO of their product, owning the business outcome, the customer relationship, the technical trade-offs, and the schedule. The paper defines the role, its authority, its boundaries with the Program Manager, and the hiring profile.
